newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. begins training Bosnian army officers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. begins training Bosnian army officers.

text.p: Retired U.S. army officers launched a training programme on Monday for Bosnian army soldiers as part of an American military aid programme for the Moslem-Croat federation.
"Two brigades began their training today," said Joseph Allred, a spokesman for the "train and equip" programme funded by the United States.
A brigade in the southwest town of Mostar and in the Sarajevo suburb of Ilijas were the first Bosnian troops to enter a 12-week training course, Allred told Reuters.

A team of 170 retired U.S. officers, from the private firm MPRI based in Alexandria, Virginia, have been hired to conduct the training programme designed to strengthen the federation military's "defensive needs", said Allred, himself of MPRI.
Retired American generals and Moslem and Croat commanders also attended the opening of a training school in Pazaric, 25 km (15 miles) south of Sarajevo, on Monday.
The training courses accompany an arms package for the federation which includes M-60 tanks, armoured personnel carriers, transport helicopters, anti-tank weapons, M-16 rifles and radios.
A small shipment of weapons arrived in August and the main shipment of 45 tanks and other military hardware should arrive on the Dalmatian coast by the end of the month, Allred said.

The $400 million programme was devised to ensure military parity in the region and help the Bosnian army counter any future threat from its Serb foes, who laid siege to Sarajevo and held more than half of Bosnia during 3-1/2 years of war.

The Moslem-led government suffered under an international arms embargo and was badly outgunned by Serb militia backed by Serbia, which seized control over most of the Yugoslav army's arsenal when the country disintegrated.
European states declined to donate to the arms programme, arguing that supplying more weapons to the region would only increase the chances of another conflict.

Military analysts say Washington's aid programme fails to provide the Bosnian army with big guns which it has always lacked. Egypt has donated 12 field guns and 12 howitzers to the "train and equip" programme to fill that need.
Without acquiring artillery, the Bosnian army would be unable to capture territory it lost during the conflict, analysts say.
The Dayton peace agreement signed last December preserved Bosnia as a loose union split between a Moslem-Croat federation and a Serb republic.
Some officers in the Bosnian army have privately criticised Washington for attaching conditions to the aid package.
U.S. officials have demanded the Sarajevo government remove Islamic foreign fighters from Bosnia and sever military ties with Iran as a condition for receiving American military aid.

Iran and some other Islamic countries supplied Bosnia with arms at a time when the Sarajevo government was desperate for military help. Some Bosnian Moslem authorities remain reluctant to cut off links with Iran.
The retired U.S. officers are also assigned the difficult task of overseeing the planned integration of still deeply mistrustful Croat and Moslem armies inside the federation.
Croats and Moslems began the Bosnian conflict as allies but later fought a fierce 10-month war for territory in central and southern Bosnia in 1993.
The two sides renewed their anti-Serb alliance under U.S. pressure but have resisted merging their armies.
Moslem and Croat authorities have appointed General Rasim Delic, a Moslem, as the commander of the federation army and General Zivko Budimir, a Croat, as his deputy.
